name: Vedapureeswarar Temple, Cheyyar
deity: Shiva as Vedapureeswarar, lord of the Vedas, with the Goddess Balakujambigai (Ilamulai Nayagi)
period: A Paadal Petra Sthalam of Thondai Nadu, the Thiruvothur of the Tevaram, sung by Sambandar (7th century)
dynasty: Thondai Nadu shrine of the Tevaram age, renewed over the centuries
summary: On the north bank of the Cheyyar river, the Lord who taught the Vedas is worshipped as Vedapureeswarar — and here, tradition says, Sambandar's hymn turned barren male palms into fruit-bearing trees.

sections.history: The town of Cheyyar in Tiruvannamalai district grew around an old sacred place, Thiruvothur, still remembered locally as Thiruvathipuram, on the northern bank of the Cheyyar river some 30 km south of Kanchipuram. Its temple to Shiva as Vedapureeswarar is one of the 276 Paadal Petra Sthalams and a Paadal Petra Sthalam of Thondai Nadu, the northern country of the Tevaram. Thirugnana Sambandar came here and sang a pathigam to the Lord, which places the shrine among the hallowed sites of the Tamil Shaiva tradition by the seventh century. The town's very name records the temple's story: tradition connects Othur with the reciting and teaching of the Vedas, for this is where the Lord is said to have revealed their meaning.
sections.architecture: The temple is built in the Dravidian manner of the Thondai country, with the Lord enshrined as a lingam in the sanctum and the Goddess Balakujambigai, known in Tamil as Ilamulai Nayagi, in a shrine of her own. In the inner prakaram a sculpture keeps the temple's best-loved story in stone: a palm tree rising beside a Shiva lingam, with Sambandar standing close by. The palm itself is honoured as the sthala vriksham, the sacred tree of the shrine — a rare choice among Shiva temples.
sections.legends: Vedapureeswarar is the Lord who, as the sthala purana tells, came to this place and imparted the Vedas, unfolding their inner meaning; from this the shrine takes both its name and its deity's title. Its other story belongs to Sambandar. A devotee who tended palms in the temple grounds grieved that every tree he had raised was male and would never bear fruit. When the child-saint came, he sang a pathigam before the Lord, and the barren male palms turned into female trees heavy with fruit — a wonder still recalled by pilgrims who stand beneath the sacred palm.
sections.festivals: The temple keeps the Shaiva year: Pradosham evenings, Maha Shivaratri, Karthigai Deepam with its lamps and Arudra Darshan in the month of Margazhi, along with the days sacred to Sambandar. Confirm festival dates locally.
sections.experience: Pilgrims come to Thiruvothur to honour the Lord who taught the Vedas and to see the palm that recalls Sambandar's hymn, and many recite his pathigam before the sanctum. The temple lies close to the main road in Cheyyar and is easily reached, so it can be joined to a day among the great shrines of Kanchipuram to the north.

visit.timings: Open daily in morning and evening sessions with a midday closure. Confirm current timings locally before visiting.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected — shoulders and knees covered; footwear is left outside before entering. Follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.photography: Photography is not permitted inside the sanctum; in the outer corridors, ask the temple staff before taking pictures, especially of rituals and the festival bronzes.
visit.gettingThere: Cheyyar lies about 30 km south of Kanchipuram and is linked by frequent buses to Kanchipuram, Arcot, Vandavasi and Chennai. Kanchipuram is the nearest convenient railway station, and Chennai International Airport, about 100 km away, is the nearest airport.
